title: A 'Counter-Intuitive' Steel Could Unlock Cheap Green Hydrogen from Seawater
summary: For green hydrogen to become a climate solution, we need electrolyzers that can handle seawater without breaking the bank. A team at the University of Hong Kong may have found the answer in a new stainless steel that defies conventional wisdom. Led by Professor Mingxin Huang, the researchers created SS-H2, a steel designed for hydrogen production. It resists corrosion at electrical potentials up to 1700 mV—far beyond the ~1000 mV limit where ordinary stainless steel fails. That's crucial because splitting water requires about 1600 mV. The secret is a 'sequential dual-passivation' strategy. Normally, stainless steel relies on a chromium oxide layer for protection. But at high voltages, that layer oxidizes into soluble Cr(VI) species, causing transpassive corrosion. SS-H2 forms a second, manganese-based passive layer on top of the chromium one at around 720 mV. This is startling because manganese is usually considered harmful to corrosion resistance. 'Initially, we did not believe it because the prevailing view is that Mn impairs the corrosion resistance of stainless steel,' said Dr. Kaiping Yu, the study's first author. 'Mn-based passivation is a counter-intuitive discovery, which cannot be explained by current knowledge in corrosion science.' The team spent six years moving from surprise to publication. The payoff could be huge. In a 10-megawatt PEM electrolysis system, structural components account for up to 53% of the HK$17.8 million cost. Replacing expensive titanium parts with SS-H2 could reduce structural material costs by about 40 times, making seawater electrolysis far more economical. This breakthrough not only advances green hydrogen but also opens a new paradigm for alloy design at high potentials.
why_it_matters: Cheap green hydrogen from seawater could accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels, helping fight climate change — and this unexpected discovery about manganese shows how challenging assumptions can lead to breakthroughs that reshape entire industries.

background_read: Green hydrogen — made by splitting water with renewable electricity — could replace fossil fuels in industry and transport. But using seawater is hard because chloride ions attack metals at high voltages. Currently, expensive titanium or platinum-coated parts are needed. Researchers at the University of Hong Kong (a leading university in East Asia) led by Professor Mingxin Huang (an expert in steel metallurgy) have spent six years developing a new stainless steel that resists this corrosion. Dr. Kaiping Yu and the team discovered that adding manganese, which experts previously thought was harmful, creates a protective shield at high voltages. This counter-intuitive result could slash the cost of electrolyzers and make green hydrogen from seawater economically viable. The breakthrough also challenges long-held assumptions in corrosion science, opening new paths for alloy design.

perspectives.description: The new steel could dramatically lower the cost of green hydrogen, making clean energy more accessible and reducing reliance on expensive materials like titanium. This could speed up the adoption of hydrogen fuel in heavy industry and long-distance transport.

The research is still at the lab scale; mass production and long-term durability in real seawater conditions need to be proven before large-scale adoption. Scaling up from a lab discovery to commercial electrolyzers often faces unforeseen engineering challenges.

This discovery upends a long-held belief in corrosion science — that manganese is always bad — highlighting how scientific progress often comes from re-examining assumptions. The dual-passivation strategy may also be applicable to other metals and extreme environments.

If successful, this steel could be used in offshore electrolysis plants, and the dual-passivation approach might inspire other alloy designs for extreme environments like space or deep-sea applications. It also sets a new benchmark for corrosion resistance in stainless steels.
